title: Echo / Auth and abuse
description: Sign-in health and signs of someone guessing passwords.

panels.title: Logins per minute
panels.description: Successful sign-ins per minute.

panels.title: Failed logins per minute
panels.description: Wrong password, or an account that does not exist.

panels.title: Failure share
panels.description: A sudden jump is a password-guessing attack, or a broken sign-in.

panels.title: Refused by the rate limiter
panels.description: Requests per minute the limiter turned away.

panels.title: Sign-in p95
panels.description: How long 95% of sign-ins took, over the selected range. Each checks the password with bcrypt (about 175 ms of CPU), so this is kept apart from the API's latency. The aim is 300 to 500 ms at most; much more than that means sign-ins are queueing for CPU.

panels.title: Sign-in latency
panels.description: Sign-in time as p50, p95 and p99. Compare with the API dashboard: a burst of sign-ins takes CPU from everything else, so a rise here is often followed by a rise there.

panels.title: Auth latency by route (p95)
panels.description: 95th percentile time for each /auth route. Sign-in is slow by design (bcrypt). Renewal and sign-out do not hash a password and should be as fast as the API's own routes.

panels.title: Auth routes: the slowest and the busiest
Auth routes, slowest first
panels.description: Every /auth route over the selected range, sorted by 95th percentile. Requests/s is the average over the range; failed is the share answered 4xx or 5xx (a wrong password is a 400, so sign-in always has some).

targets.expr: label_replace(sum by (http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{http_route=~".*/auth/.*",http_response_status_code=~"[45].."}[$__range])) / sum by (http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{http_route=~".*/auth/.*"}[$__range])) or sum by (http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{http_route=~".*/auth/.*"}[$__range])) * 0, "route", "$1", "http_route", "/api/v\\{version:apiVersion\\}(.*)")

panels.title: Requests per second by auth route
panels.description: How busy each /auth route is. Sign-in and renewal are the two that matter; the rest are rare.

panels.title: Auth requests per second by status
panels.description: Every /auth answer by HTTP status. 400 on sign-in is a wrong password or email; 429 is the rate limiter; 5xx is the API failing.

panels.title: Auth latency by route (p99)
panels.description: 99th percentile time for each /auth route: the slowest 1% of sign-ins and renewals. Next to the p95 above, a gap that widens under load means requests are queueing.

panels.title: Sign-in time, every request
panels.description: How long sign-ins took, as a distribution: one column per interval, darker is more requests. Sign-in is bcrypt, about 175 ms of CPU by design, so a band near 0.2 s is normal. A band that climbs under load is requests waiting for a core.

panels.title: Renewal time, every request
panels.description: The same for renewals. They do not hash a password, so they should sit near the API's own routes (a few ms). A band that climbs here, without a matching climb in the data routes, points at the refresh-token queries.

panels.title: API CPU in use
panels.description: Cores the API process used. The app is pinned to two cores in the load test and the production box has two, so 2 is full. Sign-in is the CPU-heavy request: compare this with the sign-in rate above.

panels.title: Thread pool queue
panels.description: Work waiting for a thread in the API. Above zero for long means the API has more to do than threads to do it, which is what sign-ins piling up looks like.

panels.title: Password checks running and waiting
panels.description: Hashes running now (at most the permit count: one less than the cores unless Hashing:MaxConcurrent is set) and hashes waiting for a permit. Waiting above zero means more people are signing in than the permits can serve; the line is capped, and past the cap sign-ins are asked to wait.

panels.title: Wait for a password check
panels.description: How long a sign-in waited for a permit before it was hashed: median, 95th and 99th percentile. Near zero is normal; seconds means a crowd is signing in.

panels.title: Sign-ins asked to wait (503)
panels.description: Password checks refused because the line was already as long as allowed, and sign-ins that answered 503 with Retry-After. The people affected try again after the time they are told.

panels.title: How long a hash takes
panels.description: The time one password hash took once it started: median, 95th and 99th percentile. The password-check line is sized on 0.2 s a hash (the dashed line): above it, a full line waits longer than 10 s and "try again in N seconds" is too short. Rises when the CPU is busy with other work. The average is the sum of hash time over the count, exact; the percentiles are read off buckets.

panels.title: Password hashes per second
panels.description: Hashes finished per second, next to the most the permits allow: permits divided by 0.2 s. A rate on the ceiling with a growing line means sign-ins are arriving faster than the box can hash them.

panels.title: Sign-ins turned away
panels.description: Share of sign-in attempts over the selected range that were answered 503 "busy" because too many password checks were waiting. Zero is normal. These people were told to try again; the server cannot see whether they did.

panels.title: Sign-ins let in and turned away
panels.description: Per minute: sign-ins that succeeded, and sign-ins refused with 503 because the password-check line was full. When the second grows, the first is at the most the server can hash.

panels.title: Gave up in the line
panels.description: Per minute: people who were waiting for a password check and gave up before it started (closed the page, lost the connection, timed out). They were in the line, so they are counted as lost.

panels.title: Closed the page during sign-in (499)
panels.description: Sign-in requests where the browser hung up before the answer, seen by nginx. Includes people who gave up in the line and people who waited out a slow answer.

panels.title: Slow auth requests (500 ms+)
panels.description: /auth requests where the work itself took 500 ms or more, over the selected range. Time spent waiting in the password-check line is left out: in a burst the line holds people for up to 10 s on purpose (see "Password check queue"), and that is not slowness. Every one is logged, starting with "slow request:". Sign-in takes about 175 ms by design.

panels.title: Slow auth requests over time, by route
panels.description: Slow /auth requests (the work took 500 ms or more, not counting time in the password-check line) per interval, by route. A rise that follows the sign-in rate up, with the line short, means sign-ins are running out of CPU.

panels.title: Slow auth requests (with trace link)
panels.description: One line per /auth request whose work took 500 ms or more, newest first: "slow request:", method, path, status and milliseconds (the total, including any time in the password-check line, which is shown as queue_wait_ms when you open the line). Open a line and use View trace to see where the time went.

panels.title: Auth log
panels.description: Everything the API logged from its auth code (sign-in failures, refresh rejections, errors) plus the slow /auth requests, newest first. Only warnings and above are kept, unless API_LOG_MIN_SEVERITY is lowered.

panels.title: Login attempts by result
panels.description: Sign-in attempts per second, split by outcome. A rise in failures can mean someone is guessing passwords.

panels.title: Failed logins by church
panels.description: Failures with no church are accounts that do not exist.

panels.title: Token refreshes and revocations
panels.description: Nothing shows until they happen.

panels.title: Password resets
panels.description: Many requests and few completions is someone probing for accounts.

panels.title: 401 and 403 responses by route
panels.description: Requests the API refused, by route. 401: not signed in or the token expired. 403: signed in but not allowed. A steady trickle of 401s is normal, because expired tokens cause them.

panels.title: Authorization decisions
panels.description: How often the API's access checks allowed or denied a request, and how often it challenged a caller who was not signed in.
